translations.text: The Book of Esther.
This happened in the days of Ahasuerus, the Ahasuerus who reigned from India to Cush over one hundred and twenty provinces.
In those days, when King Ahasuerus sat on his royal throne in Susa the citadel,
in the third year of his reign, he held a great banquet for all his officials and servants. The army of the Persians, Medes, and Parthians, and the king's officials, were before him,
along with the city's officials, while he displayed the wealth and honor of his kingdom and the glorious splendor of his greatness for many days—one hundred and eighty days.
When those days were over, the king held a seven-day banquet for all the people who remained in Susa the citadel, from the least to the greatest, in the garden courtyard of the king's palace.

Curtains of cotton and blue fabric were hung and stretched out with cords of fine linen and purple on silver rings and boxwood pillars. Couches of gold and silver stood on marble paving, with coverings of fine linen and silk.
Drinks were served in gold vessels, each vessel different from the others, and there was abundant royal wine, in keeping with the king's generosity.
The drinking followed the rule that no one was to be forced, for the king had instructed everyone in charge of his household to do as each person wished.
Queen Vashti also held a great banquet for all the women in King Ahasuerus’s royal palace.

On the seventh day, when the king was cheerful with wine, he spoke to the eunuchs: Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Teresh, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus.
He told them to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing her royal crown, to show her beauty to the peoples and the officials, because she was beautiful to look at.
But Queen Vashti would not come in at the command he sent her through the eunuchs. The king became very angry, and his fury blazed.
The king spoke to the wise men who understood the times, for this was the king's custom: he would speak before all those who understood laws and judgments,
and those close to him: Barshi, Shethar, Armath, Mos, Tarshish, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven officials of Persia and Media who sat before the king and appeared in his presence at the royal gate.
He said, “What should be done to Queen Vashti because she did not obey the command of King Ahasuerus that he sent through the eunuchs?”
Memucan said before the king and the officials, “Queen Vashti has shown contempt not only for the king, but also for all the officials and all the peoples in every province of King Ahasuerus.

When news of this matter reaches all the women, they will look down on their husbands and despise them. They will say, ‘King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti to be brought before him, but she did not come.’
Today the officials of Persia and Media who have heard the queen's response will speak [?] from all the king's officials, and all will be contempt and anger.

If it pleases the king, let a royal decree be issued by him and written among the laws of Media and Persia, so that it cannot be revoked: Queen Vashti shall never again come before King Ahasuerus, and the king shall give her royal position to another woman who is better than she.
Let the king's decree be heard and circulated throughout his whole kingdom, for it is vast. Then all women will honor their husbands, from the greatest to the least.”
This proposal pleased the king and his officials, and the king did as Memucan had proposed.

He sent letters to all the king's provinces, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language, declaring that every man should rule his own household and speak the language of his own people.
After these events, when King Ahasuerus had calmed down, he remembered Queen Vashti, everything she had done, and everything that had been decreed against her.
The king's young men and attendants said to him, “Let beautiful young women be sought for the king.

Let the king issue an order throughout all the provinces, and let them gather all the beautiful young virgins into the women's quarters, under Hegai, the eunuch in charge of the women, and let him [?] their beauty treatments.
Let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in Vashti's place.” The proposal pleased the king, and he did so.
There was a Jewish man in the citadel of Susa named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin.
He had been exiled from Jerusalem among the captives taken into exile with Jeconiah, king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had deported.

He was bringing up Hadassah, who is Esther, his uncle's daughter, because she had neither father nor mother. The young woman had a beautiful figure and was lovely in appearance. When her father and mother died, Mordecai took her as his own daughter.

When the king's decree and his command became known, and many virgins were being gathered in the citadel of Susa under the care of Hegai the eunuch, Esther too was taken to the king's palace, under the care of Hegai, the keeper of the women.

The young woman pleased him and won his favor. He hurried to provide her beauty treatments and her portions, for her and her seven maids who were to be assigned to her from the king's household. He treated her and her maids better than all the other women.
Esther did not reveal her people or her ancestry, because Mordecai had commanded her not to reveal them.
Every day Mordecai would walk in front of the courtyard of the women to find out how Esther was and what was being done to her.

When the time came for one of the young women to go before King Ahasuerus, after she had completed twelve days according to the rule for the women—for this was how the days of their beauty treatments were completed: six days with oil of myrrh and six days with perfumes and women's beauty treatments—
this was how the young woman went before the king: whatever she asked for was given to her to take with her from the women's quarters to the king's palace.

She would go in during the evening and return in the morning to the women's quarters, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch, the keeper of the concubines. She would not go before the king again unless the king desired her and summoned her by name.

When the time came for Esther, daughter of Abihail, the uncle of Mordecai who had taken her as his own daughter, to go before the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai, the king's eunuch and keeper of the women, recommended. Esther won favor in the eyes of everyone who saw her.
Esther went before King Ahasuerus in the royal palace in the tenth month, which is January, in the fourth year of his reign.
The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won his favor more than all the other virgins. She received the royal crown on her head and became queen in place of Vashti.
The king held a great banquet for all his nobles. He held a banquet for Esther, granted relief to the provinces, and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king’s gate.
Esther did not reveal her family or her people, as Mordecai had commanded her. Esther continued to obey Mordecai's command, just as she had when she was in his care.
And [?], Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the entrance, became angry and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The matter became known to Mordecai, and he revealed it to Queen Esther. Esther told the king in Mordecai's name.
The matter was investigated and found to be true. Both men were crucified on crosses, and it was recorded in the book of chronicles in the king's presence.
After these events, King Ahasuerus promoted Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and exalted him. He placed his seat above those of all the nobles who were with him.
All the king's servants at the king's gate would kneel and bow down to Haman, because the king had commanded this concerning him. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow down.
The king's servants at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why are you disobeying the king's command?"
They spoke to him every day, but he would not listen to them. So they told Haman, to find out whether Mordecai's words would stand, because he had told them that he was a Jew.
Haman saw that Mordecai would not kneel or bow down to him, and Haman was filled with rage against Mordecai.

It seemed too small a matter to lay hands on Mordecai alone, because they had told him who Mordecai's people were. Haman set his sights on all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, the people of Mordecai.
In the first month, which is Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast lots. The lots were before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, in the twelfth month, which is Adar.

Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is one people scattered and dispersed throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. Their laws differ from those of every other people, and they do not obey the king's law. It is not fitting for the king to leave them alone.

If it pleases the king, let an order be written that they be destroyed. I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those conducting the business, to be brought into the king's treasury."
The king took the signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said, “Your silver is given to you, and the people as well, to do with them whatever seems good to you.”

The king’s scribes were summoned at that time, in the first month, on the thirteenth day of the month. Everything Haman commanded was written to the king’s military commanders, to the governors in every province, and to the leaders of the peoples—to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet ring.

Letters were sent by couriers to all the king’s provinces, ordering the destruction, killing, and extermination of all the Jews, from young to old, children and women, on a single day, the thirteenth of the month of Adar, and the plundering of their possessions on that one day. It was written for the thirteenth of the month of Adar.
A copy of the document was issued in every province, commanding all the peoples to be ready for that day.
The couriers went out in haste at the king’s command, and the decree was proclaimed in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink together, while the city of Susa was in turmoil.
Mordecai learned everything that had been done. He tore his clothes, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and covered himself with ashes. He went out into the city, wailing loudly and bitterly.
He came as far as the king’s gate, but it was not lawful for anyone wearing sackcloth to enter the king’s gate.
In every province, wherever the king’s decree arrived, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping, and lamentation. Many lay in sackcloth and ashes.

Esther’s eunuchs and female servants came in and told her, and the queen was deeply distressed. She sent clothes for Mordecai to put on, so that he could take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.
Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king’s eunuchs who attended her, and sent him to Mordecai to find out what this was and why it was happening.
Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king’s gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, including the amount of silver Haman had promised to weigh out and pay into the treasury for the destruction of the Jews.
He gave him a copy of what had been decreed in the citadel of Susa to show Esther, and told him to instruct her to go to the king, appeal to him, and plead with him for her people.
Hathach went in and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Esther spoke to Hathach and instructed him to take a message to Mordecai.

All the king’s servants know that any man or woman who enters the king’s presence in the inner courtyard without being summoned faces one [?]: being put to death, except for someone to whom the king extends the golden scepter, who may live. But I have not been summoned to enter the king’s presence for three days now.
He told Mordecai what Esther had said.
Mordecai said, “Tell Esther: Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace, you alone of all the Jews will escape.

If you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s household will perish. And who knows whether it was for this very time that you were called and brought to royal power?”
Esther said, “Tell Mordecai:

Go and gather all the Jews who are in the citadel of Susa. Fast for me, and do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My young women and I will fast in the same way. Then I will enter the king’s presence, contrary to the law. If I have done it, I have done it.
Mordecai went and did everything Esther had sent word for him to do.

On the third day, Esther put on royal clothing and stood in the inner courtyard of the king’s palace, opposite the royal residence. The king was sitting on his royal throne, facing the entrance of the building.

When the king saw Queen Esther standing in the courtyard, she found favor with him. The king extended toward Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Esther approached and took hold of the tip of the golden scepter.
The king said to her, “What is it, Queen Esther? What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom will be given to you.”
Esther said, “If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come to the banquet I have prepared for him.”
The king said, “Quickly, find Haman, so that we may do as Esther has said.” So the king and Haman came to the banquet.
At the wine banquet, the king said to Esther, “What is your petition? It will be granted to you. What is your request? Even up to half the kingdom will be given to you.”
Esther answered, “My request and my petition are these:

If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases you, O king, to grant my petition and fulfill my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them tomorrow, in accordance with the king’s word.
Haman went out that day happy and glad at heart. But when Haman saw Mordecai sitting at the king’s gate, and he neither stood up nor stirred before him, Haman was filled with anger against Mordecai.
But Haman restrained himself and went home. He sent [?] for all his friends and for his wife Zeresh.
Haman told them about his splendid wealth and his many sons, and how the king had promoted him and raised him above the officials and the king’s servants.
Haman said, “Esther brought no one but me to the banquet with the king. And tomorrow too I am invited to join her with the king.
Yet all this means nothing to me whenever I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.”

His wife Zeresh and all his friends said to him, “Have a gallows made, fifty cubits high. In the morning, tell the king to have Mordecai hanged on it. Then go happily to the banquet with the king.” The suggestion pleased Haman very much, and he had the gallows made.
That night the king could not sleep. He ordered the book of records, the chronicles, to be brought in, and they read it before the king.
They found it recorded that Mordecai had reported Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the entrance, who had plotted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus.
The king said, “What honor or distinction was given to Mordecai for this?” The king’s attendants and servants said to him, “Nothing has been done for him.”
The king said, “Who is in the courtyard?” Haman had come into the outer courtyard of the king’s palace to tell the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he had prepared for him.
The king’s young attendants said to him, “Haman is standing in the courtyard.” The king said, “Let him come in.”
Haman entered, and the king said to him, “What should be done for a man whom the king wishes to honor?” Haman said to himself, “Whom would the king wish to honor more than me?”
Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king wishes to honor,
“Let them bring royal clothing that the king has worn and a horse that the king has ridden, and you should place a royal crown on his head.

Let the clothing and the horse be entrusted to one of the king’s Parthian nobles. Let them dress the man whom the king wishes to honor, mount him on the horse, and lead him around through the city streets, proclaiming before him, ‘This is what is done for the man whom the king wishes to honor!’”
The king said to Haman, “Quickly, take the clothing and bring the horse, as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king’s gate. Leave out nothing of all that you have said.”
Haman took the clothing and the horse, dressed Mordecai, and led him around through the city square, proclaiming before him, “This is what is done for the man whom the king wishes to honor!”
Mordecai returned to the king’s gate, while Haman went home mourning, with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh everything that had happened to him. His friends and his wife Zeresh said to him, “If Mordecai is of Jewish descent, and you have begun to fall before him, you cannot prevail against him. Instead, you will fall before him again.”
While he was still speaking with them, the king’s eunuchs arrived and hurried Haman off to the banquet Esther had prepared.
The king and Haman went in to the banquet that Queen Esther had prepared.
Again, on that day, at the wine banquet, the king said to Esther, “What is your request? What is your petition? Even if it is half the kingdom, it will be granted to you.”
Queen Esther answered, “If I have found favor in your eyes, O king, and if it pleases the king, let my life be granted me at my request, and my people at my petition.

For my people and I have been sold to be killed, slaughtered, and destroyed. If we had been sold to be owned as male and female slaves, I would have remained silent. For the enemy does not stop troubling the king.”
King Ahasuerus answered Queen Esther, “Who is this? Who has dared to do such a thing?”
Esther said, “The oppressor and enemy is this wicked Haman!” Haman trembled before the king and queen.

The king rose angrily from the wine banquet and went out into the palace garden. Haman stood up to plead with Queen Esther for his life, because he saw that the king had determined disaster against him.

The king returned from the palace garden to the banquet room. Haman was lying on the couch where Esther was sitting. The king said, “Will he even assault the queen here in the house with me?” As the words left the king’s mouth, Haman’s face was covered.

Harbona, one of the eunuchs, spoke up before the king: “Look, Haman also prepared a gallows on which to hang Mordecai, who spoke for the king’s benefit. It stands at Haman’s house, fifty cubits high.” The king said, “Hang him on it!”
They hanged Haman on the pole he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king’s anger subsided.
That day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king, because Esther had revealed how he was related to her.
The king took the signet ring he had taken from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman’s estate.
Esther spoke before the king again. She fell at his feet and begged and pleaded with him to undo the evil of Haman the Agagite and the plot he had devised against the Jews.
The king held out the golden scepter to Esther. Esther approached him, stood before the king, and said:

“If it pleases the king, if I have found favor in his eyes, and if the proposal seems good to the king, let him write to reverse the letters and the plans of Haman the Agagite, who wrote to destroy all the Jews throughout the king’s province.
For how can I bear to see the disaster that will befall my people? How can I bear to see the destruction of my family?”
King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther, “Look, I have given you Haman’s estate, and they have hanged him on the wooden gallows because he raised his hand against the Jews.

As for you, concerning the Jews, as you see fit, seal it in the king’s name with the king’s signet ring. A document written in the king’s name and sealed with the king’s signet ring [?] cannot be revoked.”

The king’s scribes were summoned at that time, in the third month, which is June, on the twenty-third day of the month. Everything that Mordecai wrote concerning the Jews was written to the military commanders, governors, and officials of the provinces, from Judah to Cush, 127 provinces: to each province in its own script, to each people in its own language, and to the Jews in their own script and language.
It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king’s signet ring. He sent the letters by runners and mounted messengers riding horses born of mares.

The letters that the king wrote concerning the Jews in every province allowed them to gather and defend themselves, and to destroy, kill, and wipe out everyone who attacked them, including children and women, and to take their possessions as plunder,
on a single day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar.
A copy of the document was issued in every province. It commanded all the peoples that the Jews should be ready for that day to take revenge on their enemies.
The runners and the mounted messengers riding horses went out in haste, under the decree and command issued in the citadel of Susa.
Mordecai left the king’s presence wearing royal clothing of blue and fine linen, with a gold crown, and wrapped in fine linen and purple. The city of Susa rejoiced and was glad.
For the Jews there was light and joy, honor and rejoicing.

In every province and every town, wherever the king’s decree and command arrived, there was great joy among the Jews, with feasting and celebration. Many of the peoples of the land were becoming converts, because fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.

On the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar, when the time came for the king’s decree and command to be carried out against their enemies, the situation was reversed, so that the Jews gained power over those who hated them.

The Jews gathered in their towns throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to raise their hands against those who sought to harm them. No one stood against them, because fear of them had fallen upon all the peoples.
All the officials of the provinces, the military commanders, the governors, and those who carried out the king’s business honored the Jews, because fear of the king had fallen upon them.
For Mordecai had become powerful in the king’s court, and his fame was spreading throughout all the kingdoms, because the man Mordecai was growing more and more powerful.
The Jews struck all their enemies with the sword, killing and destroying them. They did as they pleased to those who hated them.
In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men,
and Parshandatha, Dalphon, and Aspatha,
and Poratha, Adalia, and Aridatha,
and Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai, and Vaizatha.
They killed the ten sons of Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. But on that day they did not lay their hands on the plunder.
The number of those killed in the citadel of Susa was reported to the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, as well as Haman’s ten sons. What have they done in the remaining provinces? What is your petition? It will be granted to you. What is your request? It will be done for you.”
Esther said, “Let the Jews in Susa be permitted tomorrow to do as they have done today, and let Haman’s ten sons be hung on wooden gallows.”
The king said that this should be done. The command was issued in Susa, and they hanged Haman’s ten sons.
The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month and killed three hundred men in Susa, but they did not lay their hands on the plunder.

The rest of the Jews in the king’s provinces gathered and defended themselves, and gained relief from their enemies. They killed seventy-five thousand of those who hated them, but they did not lay their hands on the plunder.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and they rested on the fourteenth day of that month.
They made it a day of feasting and joy.
For this reason, the scattered Jews who live in scattered villages observe the fourteenth of Adar with joy, feasting, and celebration, and send portions to one another.
Mordecai wrote these things and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far.
requiring them to undertake to observe the fourteenth and [?] of Adar every year,

In keeping with the days on which the Jews gained relief from their enemies, and the month that was changed for them from sorrow to joy and from mourning to celebration, they were to make these days days of feasting and joy, sending portions to one another and gifts to the poor.
The Jews undertook to continue what they had begun to do and what Mordecai had written.
For Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast lots to ruin and destroy them.
When Esther came before the king, the scribe said, “Let the evil plans return upon the head of the one who plotted against the Jews, and let them hang him and his sons on wooden posts.”
For this reason they called these days Purim, after the name [?], because of the words of this letter, what they had seen, and what had happened to them.
The Jews took it upon themselves, their descendants, and everyone who joined them to observe these two days without fail, as prescribed in writing, at their appointed time every year.

These days are remembered and observed throughout all generations, provinces, and villages. These days of Purim shall not cease among the Jews, and their remembrance shall not disappear from among their descendants.
Queen Esther daughter of Abihail and Mordecai the Jew wrote down all the facts to confirm this letter concerning Purim.
He sent letters to all the Jews in the hundred and twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of King Ahasuerus, with words of truth and peace.

They were to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had established for them, and as they themselves had established for themselves and their children the command, their fasting, and their prayer.
Esther’s decree confirmed these provisions concerning Purim, which were written in the book.
King Ahasuerus imposed a tax on the whole land and on the islands of the sea.
All the deeds [?] of his power and might, and the account of the greatness of Mordecai, whom the king had promoted, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia.
For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus and was great among the Jews. He sought the good of his people and spoke on behalf of all his descendants.
